units.title: Congruency and the Geometry of Size
units.intro:
Congruent figures: same shape and size — one maps onto the other by isometries. Triangle tests: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS (right-angle, hypotenuse, side). AAA is similar, not congruent (Grade 11 similarity). AAS is ASA in disguise if you know the angle sum.

Corresponding vertices must be named in order. Tick sides and arcs on the diagram before you write a test name. Size also means perimeter and area recipes you already have — congruence says those match automatically.

cards.title: 5.1.1 Congruent figures
body: **Congruent figures** have exactly the same shape **and** the same size: if you cut one out, it fits exactly on top of the other (you may turn it over). Congruent segments have equal length; congruent angles have equal measure; two circles are congruent when their radii are equal.
Two triangles are congruent when the three sides **and** the three angles of one are equal to the **corresponding** sides and angles of the other. We write $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$.
The order of the letters is a promise: $A \leftrightarrow D$, $B \leftrightarrow E$, $C \leftrightarrow F$. From $\triangle ABC \cong \triangle DEF$ you can read off six facts:
- sides: $AB = DE$, $BC = EF$, $AC = DF$
- angles: $\angle A = \angle D$, $\angle B = \angle E$, $\angle C = \angle F$
Writing $\triangle BAC \cong \triangle DEF$ for the same triangles would be **wrong**, because it would match $B$ with $D$.
On a figure, equal sides carry the same number of **tick marks** and equal angles the same number of **arcs**.

cards.title: Matching marks show the correspondence
body: One tick: $AB = DE$; two ticks: $BC = EF$; three ticks: $CA = FD$. Same-coloured arcs mark equal angles.

cards.title: More notes
body: Write “△ABC ≅ △DEF” only when A↔D, B↔E, C↔F. Then AB=DE, angle B=angle E, and so on. Proofs: list three matching facts, name the test, then harvest more equal parts as “corresponding parts of congruent triangles.”

cards.title: 5.1.2 Tests for congruent triangles
body: You do not need to check all six parts. Any one of these sets of **three** matching parts is enough:
- **SAS (Postulate 1):** two sides and the **included** angle (the angle between those two sides).
- **ASA (Postulate 2):** two angles and the **included** side (the side between the two angles).
- **AAS (Theorem 5.1):** two angles and a side that is **not** between them. Reason: the third angles are then also equal ($180°$ minus the other two), so it becomes ASA.
- **SSS (Postulate 3):** all three sides.
- **RHS (Theorem 5.3):** in **right** triangles: the **h**ypotenuse and one other **s**ide.

**Not tests:** **AAA** — equal angles give the same shape but possibly a different size (similar, not congruent). **SSA** — two sides and a non-included angle can give two different triangles (except the right-angle case, which is RHS).

**How to write a proof:** make a two-column table (Statement | Reason). List three matching parts with a reason each (given, common side, vertical angles, alternate angles, …), name the test, and then use "corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal" to get any further fact.

cards.title: Blue sides and red angles must match
Example 5.1: a two-column proof with SAS
cards.problem: In the figure, $AO = BO$ and $CO = DO$. Prove that $\triangle AOD \cong \triangle BOC$.

steps.text: The angle is between the two sides in each triangle, so $\triangle AOD \cong \triangle BOC$ by **SAS**.
Bonus (corresponding parts): $AD = BC$ and $\angle A = \angle B$, so $AD \parallel BC$ (alternate angles).

cards.title: Example 5.2: points on the perpendicular bisector
cards.problem: $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ and meets $AB$ at $C$. $P$ is any point of $l$. Show that $PA = PB$.
cards.answer: every point of the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from $A$ and $B$

cards.title: Example 5.3: ASA with a shared angle
cards.problem: $P$ is the midpoint of $AB$; $D$ and $E$ are on the same side of $AB$ with $\angle BAD = \angle ABE$ and $\angle APE = \angle BPD$. Show $\triangle ADP \cong \triangle BEP$.

steps.text: $\angle APD = \angle APE + \angle EPD$ and $\angle BPE = \angle BPD + \angle EPD$. Since $\angle APE = \angle BPD$, adding the same $\angle EPD$ gives $\angle APD = \angle BPE$.
Two angles and the included side match: $\triangle ADP \cong \triangle BEP$ by **ASA**.

cards.title: Isosceles triangles (Theorem 5.2)
body: **Theorem 5.2:** if two sides of a triangle are equal, the angles opposite them are equal (the **base angles**). **Converse:** if two angles are equal, the sides opposite them are equal.

**Proof:** draw the bisector $AD$ of $\angle A$. Then $AB = AC$ (given), $\angle BAD = \angle CAD$ (bisector) and $AD = AD$ (common), so $\triangle ABD \cong \triangle ACD$ (SAS) and $\angle B = \angle C$.
From the same congruent triangles: $BD = DC$ and $\angle ADB = \angle ADC = 90°$. So in an isosceles triangle the bisector of the top angle is also the **median** and the **altitude** to the base.
An equilateral triangle is isosceles in every direction, so all its angles are equal: $180° \div 3 = 60°$ each.

cards.title: Example 5.5: using base angles
cards.problem: In isosceles $\triangle ABC$ with $AB = AC$, points $D$ and $E$ lie on $BC$ with $BE = CD$. Show $AD = AE$.

steps.text: $\angle B = \angle C$ — base angles of an isosceles triangle.
$BD = BE - DE$ and $CE = CD - DE$; since $BE = CD$, $BD = CE$.

cards.title: SSS and RHS
body: **SSS:** if three sides match, the triangles are congruent — a triangle is rigid: once its sides are fixed, its angles are fixed too (that is why roofs and bridges use triangles).
**RHS:** two right triangles with equal hypotenuses and one other pair of equal sides are congruent. (By Pythagoras the third sides are equal too, so it is really SSS.)

**Example:** $P$ and $Q$ are each equidistant from $A$ and $B$ ($AP = PB$, $AQ = QB$). Then $\triangle APQ \cong \triangle BPQ$ (SSS), so $PQ$ bisects $\angle APB$ and $PQ$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

cards.title: 5.1.3 Quadrilaterals and congruency
body: A **parallelogram** has both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Drawing a diagonal splits it into two congruent triangles (ASA with alternate angles and the common side) — **Theorem 5.4**. From this we get:
- **Theorem 5.5:** opposite sides are equal. **Theorem 5.7:** opposite angles are equal.
- **Theorem 5.9:** the diagonals **bisect each other**.
- Consecutive angles add up to $180°$ (co-interior angles).
Ways to **prove** that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram:
- both pairs of opposite sides equal (**Theorem 5.6**);
- one pair of opposite sides equal **and** parallel (**Theorem 5.8**);
- diagonals bisect each other; or both pairs of opposite sides parallel (definition).

Special parallelograms: a **rectangle** (all angles $90°$; a parallelogram with one right angle is already a rectangle; its diagonals are equal), a **rhombus** (all sides equal; **Theorem 5.10:** its diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other), and a **square** (both).

cards.title: Parallelogram ABCD
body: Arrows: parallel sides. Ticks on the diagonals: $AM = MC$ and $BM = MD$. Opposite angles $A$ and $C$ are equal.

cards.title: How the quadrilaterals are related
body: A square is a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time; every rectangle and every rhombus is a parallelogram. A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides, so it is not a parallelogram.

cards.title: Rhombus: diagonals cross at right angles
The mid-segment theorem (Theorem 5.11)
body: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is **parallel** to the third side and **half** as long: if $E$, $F$ are the midpoints of $AB$, $AC$ then $EF \parallel BC$ and $EF = \frac12 BC$.

**Proof idea:** extend $EF$ to $D$ with $FD = EF$. Then $\triangle AEF \cong \triangle CDF$ (SAS), so $CD = AE = EB$ and $CD \parallel AB$. So $BCDE$ is a parallelogram, giving $ED \parallel BC$ and $ED = BC$, hence $EF = \frac12 BC$.
**Example 5.7:** joining the three midpoints $D$, $E$, $F$ of the sides of a triangle cuts it into **four congruent triangles**, each similar to the big one with half its sides.

cards.title: Triangle inequality (Theorem 5.12)
body: In every triangle, the sum of any two sides is **greater** than the third side. So three lengths make a triangle only if the two shorter ones add up to more than the longest one.
- If two sides are $3$ and $7$, the third side $x$ satisfies $7 - 3 < x < 7 + 3$, i.e. $4 < x < 10$.

cards.title: Tip: SSA is a trap
body: Two sides and an angle that is **not** between them (SSA, "the donkey rule") does **not** prove congruence. The only exception is the right-angle case, which has its own name: RHS. Spell the order out loud: S-A-S has the A in the middle — the angle sits between the sides.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Two triangles $$ABC$$ and $$DEF$$ are congruent under the correspondence $$A \leftrightarrow D$$, $$B \leftrightarrow E$$, and $$C \leftrightarrow F$$. If $$AB = 2x + 3$$, $$DE = 3x - 1$$, and $$BC = 12$$, find the value of $$x$$.

steps.text: Since $$\Delta ABC \cong \Delta DEF$$ under the given correspondence, corresponding sides must be equal in length.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: In right-angled triangles $$\Delta ABC$$ and $$\Delta DEF$$, the hypotenuses are equal ($$AB = DE$$) and one pair of corresponding legs is equal ($$AC = DF$$). Which congruence criterion proves $$\Delta ABC \cong \Delta DEF$$?

steps.text: We are given two right-angled triangles $$\Delta ABC$$ and $$\Delta DEF$$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In right-angled triangles $$\Delta ABC$$ and $$\Delta DEF$$, the hypotenuses are equal ($$AB = DE$$) and one pair of corresponding legs is equal ($$AC = DF$$). Which congruence criterion proves $$\Delta ABC \cong \Delta DEF$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the given information**
We are given two right-angled triangles $$\Delta ABC$$ and $$\Delta DEF$$. The equal parts are:
- Hypotenuse: $$AB = DE$$
- One leg: $$AC = DF$$

**Step 2: Compare with congruence postulates**
The Right-Angle-Hypotenuse-Side ($$RHS$$) criterion states that if the hypotenuse and a leg of one right-angled triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and a leg of another right-angled triangle, the two triangles are congruent.

**Step 3: Match the criterion**
Since both triangles have a right angle, equal hypotenuses, and one pair of equal legs, they are congruent by the **$$RHS$$** criterion.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The correct congruence criterion is **$$RHS$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid condition for proving two triangles congruent?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** SSS, SAS, ASA (and AAS, RHS) guarantee congruence.

**Step 2:** AAA only guarantees that the triangles have the same shape (similar), not the same size.

**Step 3:** Answer: AAA.

**Tip:** SSA is also not a valid test in general.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In triangles ABC and PQR, AB = PQ, ∠B = ∠Q and BC = QR. The triangles are congruent by:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Two sides are equal (AB = PQ, BC = QR).

**Step 2:** The equal angle ∠B = ∠Q lies between those two sides (included angle).

**Step 3:** Answer: SAS.

**Tip:** In SAS the angle must be the one between the two given sides.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Two triangles $$ABC$$ and $$DEF$$ are congruent under the correspondence $$A \leftrightarrow D$$, $$B \leftrightarrow E$$, and $$C \leftrightarrow F$$. If $$AB = 2x + 3$$, $$DE = 3x - 1$$, and $$BC = 12$$, find the value of $$x$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify corresponding parts**
Since $$\Delta ABC \cong \Delta DEF$$ under the given correspondence, corresponding sides must be equal in length. Therefore:
$$AB = DE$$

**Step 2: Set up the equation**
Substitute the algebraic expressions for $$AB$$ and $$DE$$ into the equation:
$$2x + 3 = 3x - 1$$

**Step 3: Solve for $$x$$**
Subtract $$2x$$ from both sides:
$$3 = x - 1$$
Add $$1$$ to both sides:
$$x = 4$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The value of $$x$$ is **$$4$$**.

cards.title: 5.2.1 Perimeter of polygons
body: The **perimeter** of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides (the distance round the edge). For a regular polygon with $n$ sides of length $s$: $P = ns$.
**Example 5.8 idea:** for a shaded region, walk round its boundary and add every piece, including the "inside" edges that are part of the boundary; do not add edges that are not on the boundary.

**Regular polygon inscribed in a circle of radius $r$:** join the centre $O$ to two neighbouring vertices $A$, $B$. Then $\angle AOB = \frac{360°}{n}$, and the perpendicular $OE$ bisects $AB$ and the angle, so $AE = r \sin\frac{180°}{n}$ and $AB = 2r \sin\frac{180°}{n}$:
$$P_{\text{in}} = 2nr \sin\frac{180°}{n}$$
**Regular polygon circumscribed about a circle of radius $r$:** now $OE = r$ is the distance to the side (the **apothem**), so $AE = r\tan\frac{180°}{n}$:
$$P_{\text{out}} = 2nr \tan\frac{180°}{n}$$
Check with the hexagon: inscribed $P = 12r \sin 30° = 6r$ (each side equals $r$); circumscribed $P = 12r\tan 30° = 4\sqrt3\, r$.

cards.title: Inscribed and circumscribed hexagons
body: Left: $OA = OB = r$ (radius to a vertex). Right: $OE = r$ (radius to the midpoint of a side). That one difference changes $\sin$ into $\tan$.

cards.title: Examples 5.9 and 5.10: perimeters of regular polygons
cards.problem: Find the perimeter of (a) a regular decagon inscribed in a circle of radius 5 cm; (b) a regular nonagon circumscribed about a circle of radius 6 cm.

steps.text: Check: the circumscribed polygon lies outside the circle, so its perimeter is more than the circumference $2\pi r$: $39.3 > 37.7$. The inscribed one is less: $30.9 < 31.4$.

cards.title: 5.2.2 Area of polygons
body: **Area** is the number of unit squares that cover a region. The basic formulas all come from the rectangle $A = ab$:
- A diagonal cuts a rectangle into two congruent right triangles, so a **right triangle** with legs $a$, $b$ has $A = \frac12 ab$.
- **Any triangle:** $A = \frac12 bh$, where $h$ is the altitude to the base $b$ (split it into two right triangles).
- **Two sides and the included angle:** $A = \frac12 ab \sin C$ (because the altitude is $h = b \sin C$).
- **Three sides — Heron’s formula:** with $s = \frac12(a + b + c)$, $A = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$.
- **Parallelogram** $A = bh$; **trapezium** $A = \frac12(a + b)h$; **rhombus / kite** $A = \frac12 d_1 d_2$.
- **Equilateral triangle** of side $a$: $h = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}a$, $A = \frac{\sqrt3}{4}a^2$. **Regular hexagon** of side $s$: six equilateral triangles, $A = \frac{3\sqrt3}{2}s^2$.
**Composite figures:** split into triangles and rectangles (often along a diagonal), find any missing lengths with Pythagoras, then add (or subtract cut-out parts).

cards.title: Always use the perpendicular height
body: The height $h$ is always measured at right angles to the base — never along a slanting side.

cards.title: Example 5.11: area of a quadrilateral with two right triangles
cards.problem: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, $\angle ADB = 90°$, $\angle DBC = 90°$, $AB = 15$, $DC = 13$ and $BC = 5$. Find its area.

steps.text: In right $\triangle ADB$: $AD^2 = 15^2 - 12^2 = 225 - 144 = 81$, so $AD = 9$. (The textbook prints 121 and 11 here by mistake.)

cards.title: Area of regular polygons
body: Cut a regular $n$-gon into $n$ congruent isosceles triangles with apex at the centre $O$.
- **Inscribed** in a circle of radius $r$: each triangle has two sides $r$ and angle $\frac{360°}{n}$, so $A = \frac12 n r^2 \sin\frac{360°}{n}$.
- **Circumscribed** about a circle of radius $r$: each triangle has height $r$ and base $2r\tan\frac{180°}{n}$, so $A = n r^2 \tan\frac{180°}{n}$.
- With the **apothem** $a$ (distance from the centre to a side) and perimeter $P$: $A = \frac12 aP$.
Examples: hexagon inscribed in $r = 4$: $A = \frac12(6)(16)\sin 60° = 24\sqrt3$ cm². Square circumscribed about $r = 3$: $A = 4(9)\tan 45° = 36$ cm² (a $6 \times 6$ square — correct).

cards.title: 5.2.3 Arc length, perimeter and area of a sector
body: A **sector** is the "pizza slice" between two radii and an arc. Its share of the whole circle is $\frac{\theta}{360°}$, where $\theta$ is the central angle. So take that fraction of the circumference or of the area:
$$L = \frac{\theta}{360°} \cdot 2\pi r = \frac{\pi r\theta}{180°} \qquad A = \frac{\theta}{360°} \cdot \pi r^2$$
- **Perimeter of a sector** $= 2r + L$ (two radii plus the arc).
- Shortcut linking them: $A = \frac12 L r$.
- Semicircle: $\theta = 180°$; quadrant: $\theta = 90°$.
**Example 5.16:** $r = 5$, $\theta = 120°$: $L = \frac{\pi \cdot 5 \cdot 120}{180} = \frac{10\pi}{3} \approx 10.5$ cm; $P = 10 + \frac{10\pi}{3} \approx 20.5$ cm.
**Example 5.17:** $r = 6$, $\theta = 45°$: $A = \frac{45}{360}\pi(36) = 4.5\pi \approx 14.1$ square units.

cards.title: Sector and segment
body: The orange angle is the central angle $\theta$; $L$ is the arc length. The green region on the right is a segment.

cards.title: 5.2.4 Area of a segment
body: A **segment** is the region between a chord and its arc. It is the sector **minus** the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord:
$$A_{\text{segment}} = \frac{\theta}{360°}\pi r^2 - \frac12 r^2 \sin\theta$$

**Example 5.18:** $r = 5$, $\theta = 45°$: sector $= \frac{25\pi}{8}$, triangle $= \frac12(25)\sin 45° = \frac{25\sqrt2}{4}$, so segment $= \frac{25\pi}{8} - \frac{25\sqrt2}{4} \approx 9.82 - 8.84 = 0.98$ square units.
**Shaded-region problems:** area of the big shape minus the area of what is cut out (e.g. circle minus inscribed rectangle).

cards.title: Worked example: circle minus inscribed rectangle
cards.problem: A $16 \text{ cm} \times 12$ cm rectangle is inscribed in a circle. Find the area inside the circle but outside the rectangle.

steps.text: The diagonal of an inscribed rectangle is a diameter (angle in a semicircle is $90°$): $d = \sqrt{16^2 + 12^2} = 20$, so $r = 10$.

cards.title: Area formulas to know
body: Rectangle A = lw; parallelogram A = bh; triangle A = ½bh; trapezium A = ½(a + b)h; rhombus/kite A = ½d₁d₂; circle A = πr², circumference C = 2πr.
**Sector** with central angle θ: arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr, area = (θ/360°) × πr². **Segment** area = sector area − triangle area.

**Example:** a rectangle 16 cm × 12 cm is inscribed in a circle. Its diagonal √(16² + 12²) = 20 cm is a diameter, so r = 10 cm. Area of the circle outside the rectangle = π(10)² − 16 × 12 ≈ 314.2 − 192 = 122.2 cm².

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Find the area of a sector of radius 10 cm with central angle 72° (use π ≈ 3.14).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A sector of a circle of radius $$6\text{ cm}$$ has a central angle of $$120^{\circ}$$. Find the area of the sector.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the area of a sector**
The area $$A$$ of a sector with radius $$r$$ and central angle $$\theta$$ is:
$$A = \frac{\pi r^2 \theta}{360^{\circ}}$$

**Step 2: Substitute the known values**
Here, $$r = 6\text{ cm}$$ and $$\theta = 120^{\circ}$$:
$$A = \frac{\pi (6)^2 (120^{\circ})}{360^{\circ}}$$

**Step 3: Simplify the fractions**
Since $$\frac{120^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}} = \frac{1}{3}$$:
$$A = \pi \times 36 \times \frac{1}{3}$$
$$A = 12\pi\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The area of the sector is **$$12\pi\text{ cm}^2$$**.

cards.problem: A sector of a circle of radius $$6\text{ cm}$$ has a central angle of $$120^{\circ}$$. Find the area of the sector.

steps.text: **Step 1: Identify the formula for the area of a sector**
The area $$A$$ of a sector with radius $$r$$ and central angle $$\theta$$ is:

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the perimeter of a regular decagon (10-sided polygon) inscribed in a circle of radius $$5\text{ cm}$$? (Use $$\sin(18^{\circ}) \approx 0.3090$$)
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for an inscribed regular polygon**
The perimeter $$P$$ of a regular $$n$$-sided polygon inscribed in a circle of radius $$r$$ is:
$$P = 2nr \sin\left(\frac{180^{\circ}}{n}\right)$$

**Step 2: Substitute the known values**
Here, $$n = 10$$ and $$r = 5\text{ cm}$$. Therefore:
$$P = 2(10)(5) \sin\left(\frac{180^{\circ}}{10}\right)$$
$$P = 100 \sin(18^{\circ})$$

**Step 3: Calculate the numerical value**
Using the approximation $$\sin(18^{\circ}) \approx 0.3090$$:
$$P \approx 100 \times 0.3090 = 30.90\text{ cm}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The perimeter of the decagon is **$$30.90\text{ cm}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Find the area of a regular hexagon with a side length of $$4\text{ cm}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the area of a regular hexagon**
The area $$A$$ of a regular hexagon with side length $$s$$ is given by:
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^2$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$s = 4\text{ cm}$$**
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}(4)^2$$
$$A = \frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}(16)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$A = 3\sqrt{3} \times 8$$
$$A = 24\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The area of the regular hexagon is **$$24\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$$**.

lessons.title: Surface Areas and Volumes of Solid Figures

cards.title: 5.3.1 Surface area and volume of prisms
body: **Surface area** = the total area of all the faces (how much paper covers the solid; think of its net). **Volume** = the space inside, measured in cubic units ($\text{cm}^3$, $\text{m}^3$). $1$ litre $= 1000\ \text{cm}^3$ and $1\ \text{m}^3 = 1000$ litres.
**Cuboid** $l \times w \times h$: lateral area $LA = 2lh + 2wh$; base $B = lw$; total $SA = 2lh + 2wh + 2lw$; volume $V = lwh$.
**Any right prism** with base area $B$, base perimeter $p$ and height $h$:
$$LA = p \cdot h \qquad SA = 2B + ph \qquad V = Bh$$
Why $V = Bh$: one layer of unit cubes on the base holds $B$ cubes, and there are $h$ layers.

cards.title: Example 5.19: surface area of a triangular prism
cards.problem: A right prism has right-triangle bases with legs 3 cm and 4 cm, and the prism is 3 cm long. Find its total surface area and volume.

steps.text: Base area $B = \frac12(3)(4) = 6$ cm²; two bases $= 12$ cm².

cards.title: Examples 5.21 and 5.22: volumes of prisms
cards.problem: (a) A right prism of height 10 cm has an equilateral-triangle base of side 12 cm. Find its volume. (b) A tank is $120 \times 80 \times 50$ cm. How many litres does it hold?

cards.title: 5.3.2 Cylinders
body: Cut the curved surface of a cylinder straight down and unroll it: you get a **rectangle** whose length is the circumference $2\pi r$ and whose width is the height $h$.
$$LA = 2\pi r h \qquad SA = 2\pi r h + 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r(h + r) \qquad V = \pi r^2 h$$
The volume rule is the prism rule "base area × height" with base area $\pi r^2$.
**Open containers** (a cup, a tank without lid) have only one base: $SA = 2\pi rh + \pi r^2$.

cards.title: Examples 5.23 and 5.24: cylinders
cards.problem: (a) Find the total surface area of a cylinder with $r = 14$ cm, $h = 8$ cm. (b) Find the volume of a cylinder with $r = 7$ cm, $h = 20$ cm. Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.

cards.title: 5.3.3 Pyramids
body: A **regular pyramid** with an $n$-gon base of side $b$ and slant height $s$ has $n$ congruent triangular faces, each of area $\frac12 bs$:
$$LA = \frac12 n b s \qquad SA = LA + B \qquad V = \frac13 Bh$$
- Find a missing slant height with Pythagoras: $s^2 = h^2 + \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2$ (square base).
- Why $\frac13$: a cube can be cut into **three** congruent square pyramids with the same base and height as the cube, so each is one third of the cube.
- Do not mix $h$ (height, used for volume) with $s$ (slant height, used for surface area).

cards.title: Examples 5.25 and 5.26: pyramids
cards.problem: (a) A regular square pyramid has base 10 cm and height 9 cm. Find its total surface area. (b) A regular triangular pyramid has height 12 cm and base edges 8 cm. Find its volume.

cards.title: 5.3.4 Cones
body: Unroll the curved surface of a cone: you get a **sector** of a circle with radius $s$ (the slant height) and arc length $2\pi r$. Its area is $\frac12 \times \text{arc} \times \text{radius} = \frac12(2\pi r)s = \pi rs$.
$$s = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2} \qquad LA = \pi r s \qquad SA = \pi r s + \pi r^2 \qquad V = \frac13 \pi r^2 h$$
A cone holds one third of the cylinder with the same base and height — just as a pyramid holds one third of its prism.

cards.title: Unrolling a cone gives a sector
Examples 5.27 and 5.28: cones
cards.problem: (a) A cone has $r = 6$ cm and $h = 8$ cm. Find its total surface area. (b) A cone has height 12 cm and base diameter 10 cm. Find its volume. Use $\pi = 3.14$.

cards.title: 5.3.5 Spheres
body: Archimedes showed that a sphere of radius $r$ fits exactly in a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $2r$, and:
- the surface of the sphere equals the curved surface of that cylinder: $2\pi r \cdot 2r$;
- the sphere fills $\frac23$ of the cylinder: $\frac23 \cdot \pi r^2 \cdot 2r$.
$$SA = 4\pi r^2 \qquad V = \frac43 \pi r^3$$
**Hemisphere** (half a sphere): $V = \frac23 \pi r^3$; curved surface $2\pi r^2$; a solid hemisphere also has a flat circle, so total $3\pi r^2$.
Watch the diameter: always halve it first.

cards.title: Same radius r and height 2r
body: Cone : sphere : cylinder $= 1 : 2 : 3$ in volume ($\frac23\pi r^3 : \frac43\pi r^3 : 2\pi r^3$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Find the volume of a sphere of radius $$3\text{ cm}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for the volume of a sphere**
The volume $$V$$ of a sphere with radius $$r$$ is given by:
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$r = 3\text{ cm}$$**
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (3)^3$$
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi (27)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$V = 4\pi \times 9$$
$$V = 36\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The volume of the sphere is **$$36\pi\text{ cm}^3$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A right circular cylinder has a radius of $$7\text{ cm}$$ and a height of $$10\text{ cm}$$. Find its total surface area. (Take $$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$$)
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the formula for total surface area of a cylinder**
The total surface area $$SA$$ of a cylinder is:
$$SA = 2\pi rh + 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r(h + r)$$

**Step 2: Substitute the given values**
Here, $$r = 7\text{ cm}$$, $$h = 10\text{ cm}$$, and $$\pi = \frac{22}{7}$$:
$$SA = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times (10 + 7)$$

**Step 3: Simplify the expression**
$$SA = 24 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 17$$
$$SA = 44 \times 17$$
$$SA = 748\text{ cm}^2$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The total surface area of the cylinder is **$$748\text{ cm}^2$$**.

cards.q: A cone has base radius 3 cm and height 4 cm. What is its volume (in terms of π)?
cards.why: V = ⅓πr²h = ⅓ × π × 9 × 4 = 12π cm³. (36π is the cylinder with the same base and height — the cone is one third of it.)

questions.q: Given $\triangle MQP \cong \triangle NOR$, list the six pairs of corresponding equal parts.
questions.answer: $MQ = NO$, $QP = OR$, $MP = NR$; $\angle M = \angle N$, $\angle Q = \angle O$, $\angle P = \angle R$
why: Step 1: match letters in order: $M \leftrightarrow N$, $Q \leftrightarrow O$, $P \leftrightarrow R$.
Step 2: sides use pairs of letters in the same positions: $MQ = NO$, $QP = OR$, $MP = NR$.
Step 3: angles: $\angle M = \angle N$, $\angle Q = \angle O$, $\angle P = \angle R$.
questions.tip: Write the two names one above the other and read down the columns.
